traditions/american-baptist-churches-usa: Heirs of the northern Baptist mission societies (Triennial Convention 1814; Home Mission Society 1832) that remained after the 1845 Southern split. Organised as the Northern Baptist Convention (1907), renamed the American Baptist Convention (1950) and American Baptist Churches USA (1972). A theologically diverse, ecumenical body, it was the church of Walter Rauschenbusch and a founding member of the Federal, National and World Councils of Churches; it ordains women.
Historic home of the Social Gospel
Wide theological range from evangelical to liberal
Scripture as the authoritative witness to Christ, interpreted in freedom of conscience; no binding confession.
Salvation through faith in Jesus Christ; emphasis on personal and social transformation.
Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Varied; classical hope of Christ's return and the kingdom of God.

Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. Regional associations and national boards.
Free-church services with hymns, preaching and lay participation.
Active; roughly 1.1 million members reported in recent years, with several regions having left over sexuality debates.
traditions/seventh-day-baptists/summary: Baptists who keep the seventh day (Saturday) as the Sabbath. Sabbatarian Baptist congregations appeared in England in the 1650s (Mill Yard, London); the first American church was organised at Newport, Rhode Island, in 1671. Seventh Day Baptist teaching on the Sabbath influenced the early Adventists in the 1840s.
traditions/seventh-day-baptists/distinct: Early Sabbatarian witness in England and New England
Link to the Adventist adoption of the Sabbath (Rachel Oakes Preston, 1844)
traditions/seventh-day-baptists/profile/: Scripture alone; the Bible's commandment of the seventh-day Sabbath taken as still binding.
Salvation by grace through faith; Sabbath-keeping as grateful obedience, not a means of salvation.
Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Expectation of Christ's return and judgment.

Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. A General Conference (1802) and a World Federation link churches.
Saturday worship with preaching and hymns.
traditions/seventh-day-baptists/status: Active but small; congregations in North America, Africa, Asia and Latin America linked by the Seventh Day Baptist World Federation.
traditions/free-will-baptists/summary: Arminian Baptists in the General Baptist line. Paul Palmer organised a church in Chowan County, North Carolina, in 1727, and Benjamin Randall founded a northern Free Will Baptist movement at New Durham, New Hampshire, in 1780. The northern body merged with the Northern Baptists in 1911; southern churches formed the National Association of Free Will Baptists in 1935.
traditions/free-will-baptists/distinctiv: Feet washing as an ordinance in many churches
traditions/free-will-baptists/profile/au: Scripture alone; the Treatise of the Faith and Practices of Free Will Baptists.
traditions/free-will-baptists/profile/sa: Christ died for all; salvation is conditioned on faith, and a believer may forfeit salvation by unbelief.
Believers' baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and, in many churches, washing of the saints' feet.
traditions/free-will-baptists/profile/es: Expectation of Christ's return, judgment and eternal destinies.
traditions/free-will-baptists/profile/go: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions.
traditions/free-will-baptists/profile/wo: Revivalist and gospel-song services; communion often followed by feet washing.
traditions/free-will-baptists/status: Active; National Association of Free Will Baptists and related bodies.
traditions/nigerian-baptist-convention/s: Grew from the Southern Baptist mission of Thomas Jefferson Bowen, who reached Yorubaland in 1850, and from Yoruba Baptist leaders who carried the work forward when American missionaries withdrew during the U.S. Civil War. The Yoruba Baptist Association (1914) became the Nigerian Baptist Convention, one of the largest Baptist bodies outside the United States. African Baptist churches also arose from the 1888 'Native Baptist' secession over missionary control.
traditions/nigerian-baptist-convention/d: Evangelism across Nigeria and West Africa
traditions/nigerian-baptist-convention/p: Scripture alone; Baptist confessional statements adapted from Southern Baptist models.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.

Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. Conferences and an elected president and general secretary.
Yoruba and English services with choirs, indigenous music and preaching.
traditions/nigerian-baptist-convention/s: Active; one of the largest member bodies of the Baptist World Alliance, with membership reported in the millions.
traditions/brazilian-baptist-convention/: Formed in 1907 from churches planted after Southern Baptist missionaries William and Anne Bagby and Zachary and Kate Taylor organised the first Portuguese-speaking Baptist church in Salvador, Bahia, in 1882. Brazilian Baptists became one of the largest Baptist communities in the world and sent missionaries abroad; a charismatic wing separated in 1965 as the National Baptist Convention (CBN).
Strong home and foreign mission boards
Scripture alone; Brazilian Baptist Declaration of Faith.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions.
Evangelistic services with congregational singing and preaching.
Active; a major member body of the Baptist World Alliance.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/summary: A movement of believers who began meeting simply to 'break bread' outside the established churches in Dublin in the late 1820s; the large assembly at Plymouth (from 1831) gave the movement its popular name. Leaders included Anthony Norris Groves, B. W. Newton, George Müller and John Nelson Darby, whose dispensationalism and pre-tribulation rapture teaching spread far beyond the Brethren. They divided in 1848 into Open and Exclusive branches.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/distinctive: No ordained clergy; open participation of brothers in worship
Gathering in the name of the Lord alone, without denominational labels
traditions/plymouth-brethren/profile/aut: Scripture alone, studied by all believers; no creeds.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/profile/sal: Salvation by grace through faith, with strong assurance.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/profile/sac: Believers' baptism (mostly immersion) and the weekly Lord's Supper as remembrance.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/profile/esc: Dispensational premillennialism, with a pre-tribulation rapture.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/profile/gov: Local assemblies led by a plurality of elders; no clergy-laity distinction.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/profile/wor: Unstructured worship meeting around the Lord's Table, with participation by men; women usually silent and head-covered.
traditions/plymouth-brethren/status: Active in Open and Exclusive branches worldwide.
traditions/open-brethren/summary: The branch of the Brethren that, after the 1848 Bethesda controversy, treated each assembly as independent in receiving members and exercising discipline. Open Brethren became a major source of 'faith' missionaries, including Anthony Norris Groves in India and F. S. Arnot in central Africa (Echoes of Service), and are numerous in India, Zambia, Angola and Latin America.
traditions/open-brethren/distinctives/1: Open reception of believers to the Lord's Table
traditions/open-brethren/distinctives/2: Faith missions (Echoes of Service, Christian Missions in Many Lands)
traditions/open-brethren/profile/salvati: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
traditions/open-brethren/profile/sacrame: Believers' baptism by immersion and weekly breaking of bread.
traditions/open-brethren/profile/governa: Autonomous assemblies led by elders; some now employ full-time workers.
traditions/open-brethren/profile/worship: Breaking of bread meeting with open participation, plus preaching services.
traditions/open-brethren/status: Active; especially strong in India, Zambia, Angola, Latin America and the English-speaking world.
traditions/exclusive-brethren/summary: The branch of the Brethren following John Nelson Darby after 1848, holding that assemblies form one connected fellowship whose disciplinary decisions bind all. Further divisions followed; the largest present body, the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church (formerly the Taylor–Symington–Hales line), practises strict separation from non-members, which critics and former members describe as harmful to family relationships and which the church defends as biblical holiness.
traditions/exclusive-brethren/distinctiv: Interconnected assemblies bound by common discipline
Separation from evil as a principle of unity
Some branches practise strict social separation
traditions/exclusive-brethren/profile/au: Scripture alone, with Darby's writings and those of later leading teachers highly valued.
traditions/exclusive-brethren/profile/sa: Baptism (in some branches including household baptism of children) and weekly Lord's Supper.
traditions/exclusive-brethren/profile/go: Fellowship of assemblies; in some branches a recognised universal leader.
traditions/exclusive-brethren/profile/wo: Lord's Supper and ministry meetings; men speak, women head-covered.
traditions/exclusive-brethren/status: Active in several separate fellowships; the PBCC is the largest.
traditions/church-of-the-brethren/summar: Founded in 1708 when Alexander Mack and seven others baptised one another in the river Eder at Schwarzenau, combining Radical Pietism with Anabaptist convictions. Persecuted in Europe, the Brethren ('Dunkers') moved to Pennsylvania from 1719. One of the three historic peace churches, with a large church in Nigeria (Ekklesiyar Yan'uwa a Nigeria, EYN) that has suffered heavily from Boko Haram attacks.
traditions/church-of-the-brethren/distin: Love feast with feet washing, fellowship meal and communion
No force in religion; no creed but the New Testament
Simple living and service (Brethren Volunteer Service, Heifer Project origins)
traditions/church-of-the-brethren/profil: The New Testament as the rule of faith and practice, read in community; no formal creed.
Salvation by grace received in faith and lived in obedient discipleship.
Believers' baptism by trine immersion; the love feast, combining feet washing, a fellowship meal and the bread and cup; anointing of the sick.
Hope of Christ's return; little speculative emphasis.
Congregational with an Annual Conference as the highest authority.
Simple services; love feast observed periodically.
traditions/church-of-the-brethren/status: Active; the U.S. church has declined, while EYN in Nigeria is larger.
traditions/brethren-in-christ/summary: Arose about 1778 among Mennonite and Pietist believers in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania (the 'River Brethren', after the Susquehanna), who sought a personal conversion experience alongside Anabaptist discipleship. From the 1910s it absorbed Wesleyan holiness teaching. Its largest membership today is in Zimbabwe, Zambia and other African and Asian countries.
traditions/brethren-in-christ/distinctiv: Blend of Anabaptist, Pietist and Wesleyan holiness streams
Strong missions in southern Africa and India
traditions/brethren-in-christ/profile/au: Scripture as final authority, interpreted in community.
traditions/brethren-in-christ/profile/sa: New birth by grace through faith, followed by sanctification and discipleship.
Believers' baptism by trine immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
traditions/brethren-in-christ/status: Active; member of Mennonite World Conference.
